chapter_theme: What makes a king excellent: not power alone but a set of resources and qualities that must be held without lapse, and above all how he is to the people who approach him. His standing is conferred from below, by those who praise him, shelter under him, and set him apart.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar opens with the six limbs of a kingdom (381), then treats the king's excellence (382-385) and excellence together with its fruits (386-390).

381.reading: One who has all six, an army, a people, resources, ministers, allies and a fort, stands among kings as the male leads its herd.
381.nuance: ஏறு names the male of a species, not specifically a lion. Pope's and Kalaignar's lion is an interpretive choice. Parimelazhagar presses ஆறும்: lacking even one limb, royal policy doesn't function.

382.reading: Fearlessness, giving, understanding and drive, these four never failing, are the nature of a king.
382.nuance: The weight is on எஞ்சாமை. Parimelazhagar explains that when one quality surfaces in a person others recede, and a king can't afford that, so the verse asks for constancy as well as possession.

383.reading: Promptness, learning and resolve: these three do not leave those who rule the land.

positions.position: துணிவு here stands for manly swiftness, acting quickly without regard to anything else.
துணிவு is a settled decision reached after examining the matter.

384.reading: A king does not stray from virtue, removes what is not virtue, and keeps an honour that does not stray from valour.
384.nuance: The verse pairs அறன் with மறன், so virtue and martial valour stand side by side as parts of one honour. Parimelazhagar illustrates this honour with rules of war, such as not striking the young, the old or one who flees.

positions.position: What is removed is wrongdoing in his realm, such as killing and theft. It is a public duty.
positions.quote: அறனல்லவை தன் நாட்டின் கண்ணும் நிகழாமல் கடிந்து

positions.position: What is removed is desire and anger, the king's own inner faults.

385.reading: A king is one able to create sources of wealth, gather it, guard it, and apportion what is guarded.
385.nuance: Four verbs form a cycle that ends in distribution, not in holding. The verse doesn't say to whom. Parimelazhagar spreads the giving over virtue, wealth and pleasure, while Manakkudavar's example is equipping the army.

386.reading: If a king is easy to see and not harsh of speech, his land is spoken of above others.
386.nuance: The grammar praises the land, not the king. Parimelazhagar notes that praising the land makes praising the king unnecessary, though he has to supply the world as the speaker.

387.reading: For those who can give and protect with pleasant words, this world falls in with their word and their intent.
387.nuance: The second line is compressed, and my reading of தன் சொலால் தான் கண்டனைத்து is tentative. Pleasant speech is named as what makes the giving work, not as an extra.

positions.position: சொல் means fame: the world, joined to his renown, becomes as much as he conceives.
positions.quote: இவ்வுலகம் தன் புகழோடு மேவித் தான் கருதிய அளவிற்றாம்

positions.position: சொல் means his command: by it the world lies in his control.
positions.quote: தன்னேவலாலே இவ்வுலகம் தான் கண்டாற்போலும் தன் வசத்தே கிடக்கும்

388.reading: The ruler who does justice and protects is set apart as இறை for the people.
388.nuance: வைக்கப்படும் is passive and conditional: the status is awarded for doing justice, not held by right of office.

positions.position: Though a man by birth, by his deeds he is placed apart as a god for humans.
positions.quote: பிறப்பான் மகனேயாயினும், செய்வான் மக்கட்குக் கடவுள் என்று வேறு வைக்கப்படும்

positions.position: He is reckoned the lord of people, a political headship with no deification.
He is honoured as the people's leader.

389.reading: The world rests under the parasol of a king with the character to bear words that are bitter to the ear.
389.nuance: செவிகைப்ப moves a taste onto the ear, as Parimelazhagar points out. Tolerance of bitterness is presented as what brings the world under the parasol, which reverses the usual picture of power as not having to listen.

positions.position: The words are the rebukes of counsellors, borne for the good they will produce.
positions.quote: இடிக்கும் துணையாயினார் சொற்களைத் தன் செவி பொறாதாகவும்.

positions.position: The words are reports of what others have done wrong, and the king forgives those offences. He also records a view that they are a priest's words.
positions.quote: பிறர் செய்த குற்றங்களைக் கேட்டு வைத்தும், அதனைப் பொறுக்கவல்ல குணமுடைய

390.reading: One who has these four, giving, kindness, a straight sceptre and care of the people, is a light among kings.
390.nuance: Manakkudavar reads all four as relief for struggling farmers, including seed and plough and deferred or waived dues. That makes the verse far more concrete than its abstract nouns suggest.

links.note: The king must never lack அஞ்சாமை, yet 428 calls not fearing what should be feared folly. Read together, kingly fearlessness can't mean fearing nothing.
தூங்காமை is a permanent royal quality here. 672 uses the same word to divide tasks: some should be slept on and some should not. The trait becomes a judgment about each case.
467 fixes the order, deliberate and then resolve, which supports Manakkudavar's reading of துணிவு here and sits uneasily with Parimelazhagar's action without regard to anything.
The negative of the same pair. Being hard to see and harsh of look turns great wealth into what a demon has found: 386 gives the praise, 565 the horror.
The same verb, வைக்கப்படும், raises a just ruler to இறை and a rightly living householder among the gods. Both are placed there by how they live, one in public and one at home.
389 asks the king to bear bitter words; 448 says what follows if no one speaks them: he falls with no enemy needed. Parimelazhagar's gloss on 389 uses the same idea of இடிக்கும் துணை.

source_issues: 382: Parimelazhagar's gloss reads தீமையும் where the word glossed is அஞ்சாமை. It is probably a corruption, perhaps of திண்மையும், so I did not rely on it.
